text: Resident Evil: 2026's pro-life horror romp. An inspired, fun, and quick journey, Zach Cregger realizes the that the best was to adapt the titular videogame series is to not directly adapt it at all. Instead of backflips, quips, and that dastardly Albert Wesker, we get the worst night in one guy's simple life, à la Martin Scorsese's After Hours. Resident Evil doesn't overstay its welcome, although the comedy does get to be grating come the second half, and the horror somewhat fizzles out. Still, knowing the crazy stories and lore about the franchise (and being forever stuck in one of the spinoff games), Resident Evil is best as a spiritual adaptation rather than trying to put Leon Kennedy's tramp-stamped self in a cohesive narrative. The actual evil residents were the guys laughing at that poor kid getting shot in the RV.

text: Birth of auteur theory was (partially) predicated on the question of whether a director can get their authorship through the studio factory, industry. At this point we have seen this happen time and time again as the entire meta shifted since this theory was first espoused. Now, the modern equivalent would be: Can a director still maintain their authorship while making a movie rooted in a pre-existing IP? We have seen examples of this, ‘Aliens’ (1986) is the first that comes to mind. But... that was a long time ago. And yeah, I'm excited for the upcoming Godzilla movie... I'm not anti-franchise. Simply, ‘Resident Evil’ isn't as good as ‘Barbarian’ or ‘Weapons’ and it's easy to imagine how jumping through hoops of whatever Resident Evil means only hindered the movie. I would have much rather Creggers made his own zombie movie. Or an actual Resident Evil movie (beyond the occasional fandering, this is more survival horror than RE.) Of which... the character cheering and exclaiming “video games!” is one of the cringiest moments in movie history. Let's be honest... this is more of an homage to video games than Resident Evil. Everything up until the main character leaving the tunnel and getting into the car was awesome. I loved that feeling of isolation! It was fun but by the finale it just felt weightless. Cotton candy movie.

text: The movie is fantastic, but it does falter slightly towards the end. I’ll begin by stating that I am a HUGE Resident Evil fan and really enjoyed Cregger’s previous films. I was initially skeptical when Cregger mentioned that the movie resembles a survival horror experience, but he managed to pull it off remarkably well! The entire movie feels like the main character is just barely surviving, and you can feel the tension and urgency the entire time. I was surprised how well the comedy in the movie actually worked. Leave it to somebody who made his career in comedy to make actual funny interactions that fit in so well with the events of the movie. Austin Abrams did a great job playing a lovable, hapless, bumbling idiot; he is no Leon, Chris, but he still feels like a Resident Evil character just in a way I can't explain. Overall the movie was awesome and what I wanted and I love it for that. The only thing I wasn’t the biggest fan of was the end. I don’t know why and can't really put it into the right words, but it just felt weird and sudden, I guess, and something about it rubbed me the wrong way. text: "Here's the thing about magic. It won't be silenced." This was much better than I anticipated. The tributes to the original were beautifully crafted into the film, and not overly forced or a complete mimic (which I find some sequels do these days). It also felt very natural and true to the first Practical Magic, with the storyline being realistic in the sense of how characters behaved, their lifestlyes, and their adaptation to the contemporary world It was equally nice to watch a modern film where you couldn't always expect what would happen next. I loved seeing the Owen's sisters back on the screen, and the whole witchy aesthetic and vibe-especially coming up to Halloween. The original is definitely more the iconic and comfort movie of the two, but I wouldn't say this film is significantly behind.
